title_en: Otterly delightful: rare Malaysian wildlife returns to once-polluted Kuala Lumpur river
content_en:
The presence of the smooth-coated otters has raised hopes that efforts to clean up the Klang River may be bearing fruit.
A smooth-coated otter eats a fish along the bank of the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur on October 19. Photo: AFP
Beneath a tangle of highway in the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur, a family of otters rolls around in a patch of riverside sand, delighting the few passers-by who notice them.
Small groups of otters are now being seen regularly in parts of the city, including along the once heavily polluted Klang River.
Theories vary on whether the smooth-coated otters, classed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, have returned to the city or were hiding in plain sight all along. But their presence has raised hopes that efforts to clean up the Klang may be bearing fruit, and could inspire further improvement.
The Klang was once one of the world’s dirtiest waterways, designated a Class 5 severely polluted river under Malaysia’s rankings. Years of work improved it to Class 3, or moderately polluted, which seems to have encouraged the otters to move in, said Malaysian wildlife ecologist Woo Chee Yoong.
“Wherever there are otters, there are fish. Wherever there are fish it means the whole river system … [is] clean, it’s healthy for all the communities around. So that’s one of the importance of otters,” he said.
Smooth-coated otters play on the bank of the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur on October 19. Photo: AFP
In recent years, the animals have been filmed sunbathing on the river’s concrete banks and swimming in front of elevated metro stations, winning viral fame.
Retired soldier Hasan Ujang, who lives in a riverside flat, enjoys watching their antics. “We feel really happy when we watch them playing and playing, like kids swimming,” he said.
But unlike otters in neighbouring Singapore, which are closely monitored by a network of citizen scientists, little is known about Kuala Lumpur’s otters.
Woo learned about them from local media reports on sightings in 2019 and the following year co-founded the Malaysian Otter Network (MON) conservation group.
“We don’t know how many groups are there, we don’t know how actually the otters are moving around,” he said. Even the question of whether the otters have returned to the capital or were simply in less visible city environments before remains a “mystery”.
MON hopes to set up a citizen science system for people to report sightings.
Nuisance or asset?
Otters have been spotted elsewhere in the city, including at the Tropicana Golf & Country Resort, a high-end housing estate where they are less welcome visitors. They are accused of raiding at least 12 houses in the past year. Their target: fish ponds.
Resident Yee Sze Mun, 89, said otters killed the beloved – and expensive – arowana fish he had nurtured for 15 years. “They are a nuisance, but I can’t blame them, because they are just like us, they have to survive,” he said.
Residents say the incursions began last year after a company began clearing forest next door for a new development.
“We have an issue because they’re losing their habitat,” said residents’ association president Joy Appukuttan, who called the otter attacks a “grave concern”.
Wildlife ecologist and co-founder of the Malaysian Otter Network conservation group Woo Chee Yoong uses binoculars to spot smooth-coated otters along the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur. Photo: AFP
Tropicana’s security team believes there are around 25 otters in the forest and the estate brought in Woo to teach residents how to deal with them. The species is protected in Malaysia, so Woo urges residents to block entry points to their gardens and install fences or netting over ponds.
Maimunah Mohd Sharif, a former Kuala Lumpur mayor and now adviser to the city on sustainable urbanisation, called the otters an “asset”.
“Otters are one of the benchmarks for clean cities,” she said.
Like others, she hopes a growing awareness of the Klang River otters can be harnessed to help improve the river further.
Hundreds of garbage traps were installed as part of the government’s River of Life project, and solar-powered “interceptors” deployed by a Dutch NGO have collected tens of thousands of tonnes of waste.
Architect and co-organiser of the annual Klang River Festival Scarlett Koon stands around her project site in Kuala Lumpur. Photo: AFP
Now Maimunah wants to see more done to stop waste entering the river in the first place, and efforts to make the Klang Class 2B status, clean enough for body contact. “One day, I want to swim in the Klang River,” she said.
Scarlett Koon Si Qi, a community architect and co-organiser of the annual Klang River Festival, hopes the waterway can be restored to its natural banks without concrete lining.
“Some parts, maybe yes, you do need concrete to kind of protect and control for floods,” she said. “But I think wherever we can, we should leave it as natural as possible.”
That would further benefit the otters, who need some vegetation and natural crevices to hide in, experts said.
The otters are already shifting views on the river, said Faith Foo, who runs the festival.
Growing up, “the teachers would always say that this is a very unsanitary place,” he said. But seeing the otters, “it’s a reminder that that is a river”.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Beijing hails Election Committee poll for affirming ‘patriots-only’ system in Hong Kong
content_en:
Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO) says record turnout in city reflects growing maturity of ‘patriots-only’ system to elect good candidates.
Elected candidates pose for pictures on stage at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre (HKCEC) on Sunday. Photo: Sam Tsang
Beijing has lauded Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll for demonstrating what it called the broad representation, political inclusiveness and fair competition of the “patriots-only” system, saying the latest race proved the effectiveness of the model.
In a statement issued on Monday, the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO) also said the poll – which drew a record turnout of nearly 99 per cent, or 5,640 registered voters – reflected that the revamped electoral system was now operating with “increasing maturity” and strengthening people’s confidence in building “high-quality democracy” in the city.
The overall turnout of the Sunday poll jumped by about 9 percentage points from 2021, as 856 candidates competed for 723 seats in the 1,500-strong powerful electoral college tasked to choose the city’s next leader.
Several prominent business and professional leaders lost out in tighter races for seats on the body.
“The Election Committee election once again demonstrates that the new electoral system possesses broad representation, political inclusiveness, balanced participation and fair competition, truly achieving the goal of electing capable and virtuous individuals,” an HKMAO spokesman said.
He pointed to the greater competition in the election, citing the diverse backgrounds of the candidates, which included veterans and newcomers, representatives from mainland China, and leaders of local and foreign companies.
The office said the latest poll reflected that the electoral system – revamped five years ago in the wake of the 2019 social unrest to ensure only patriots hold political power – had matured and boosted residents’ confidence.
“It proved again that the new electoral model is a good system that fits the ‘one country, two systems’ blueprint and Hong Kong’s actual situation, as well as one which promotes the city’s healthy democratic development,” the spokesman said.
The HKMAO called on the members of the powerful committee to use their strengths and influence and unite residents from all walks of life in giving full support to the government.
A large advertisement for the 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections at Wanchai Tower. Photo: Nora Tam
In a separate statement, Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong also said that the Election Committee poll had, through its nominations and turnout, as well as candidates’ backgrounds and campaign atmosphere, showcased “quality democracy”.

title_en: China undertaker recalls toughest case: 2 days restoring accident victim’s face from photo
content_en:
Years of handling countless cases have made illness and death familiar to Zhou, yet unexpected deaths remain painful.
Zhou often practises suturing techniques to restore his clients’ appearance and preserve their dignity. Photo: Handout
An award-winning young Chinese undertaker has shared the cases that have stayed with him, saying his greatest inspiration is that “nothing matters except life and death.”
Zhou Wang, 32, has worked as an undertaker at Hangzhou Funeral Home in Zhejiang province, eastern China, for more than a decade. He won the title of “Gold Medal Mortuary Cosmetologist” at a provincial competition in 2022 and was named the city’s “civil affairs craftsman” the following year.
Reflecting on his decade-long career, Zhou said the case he remembered most involved a man who accidentally fell into an industrial mixer.
The man’s son’s greatest wish was to see his father’s face one more time. They had last seen each other two years earlier, at the son’s wedding.
Zhou said the man’s body had been completely destroyed in the mixer, so the team could not guarantee they could fully restore his face.
He and two colleagues spent 48 hours cleaning, filling, joining and applying make-up to the man’s face, using a photograph as a reference.
Zhou noted that death feels less frightening when people in the field treat it as a profession, not a taboo. Photo: Handout
Zhou recalled the son telling them that they had restored his father’s face as he remembered it.
In another case, the team applied make-up to a teenager who had died of leukaemia, making him look as he had before his illness, when he was healthy and sporty, to bring his parents some comfort.
Despite his relatively young age, Zhou has learned from experience that a final farewell is always tinged with regret – and that he is no exception.
He has handled the funerals of his own family members, including his grandparents and his mother-in-law, who never looked down on him because of his profession. On the contrary, she continued to support his relationship with her daughter, a nurse.
When she died, he spent a long time sitting in his workroom, bidding her farewell.
Zhou said that his work and his wife’s both reflect a deep respect and reverence for life.
After handling countless cases over the years, Zhou said he had grown accustomed to illness and death, but still found unexpected deaths difficult to bear.
He said he was particularly affected by the case of a young woman who took her own life after hearing a few harsh words from her family.
Zhou said that both his and his wife’s work is guided by a deep respect for life. Photo: Shutterstock
“Be strong. Live well. Nothing matters except life and death,” Zhou said, summing up what his work had taught him.
Zhou studied modern funeral technology and management at a vocational college in Beijing. At the time, he chose the major because it offered a relatively stable career path, but his father kept telling him to “stick to it and not give up halfway if you choose this profession.”
That became one of his mottos. He also continued learning new skills, including make-up techniques from beauty vloggers.
Zhou said the current trend is to give the deceased a more lifelike appearance with cosmetics. At families’ request, the team may even highlight features such as cute under-eye bags or reshape the eyebrows.
He admitted that he felt pressured to learn new make-up techniques as more young women in their 20s and 30s entered the industry.
“Death is less frightening when people in the industry treat it as a profession rather than a taboo,” Zhou said, reflecting on his work.
“This profession does such meaningful work, allowing the deceased to leave this world with dignity,” one online observer remarked.
“It is a very respectable profession that requires an exceptionally strong and kind heart,” another commented.

title_en: China’s memory chipmakers are catching up to industry leaders. What happens when they do?
content_en:
CXMT and YMTC are the twin pillars of China’s memory self-sufficiency drive amid US export restrictions.
Illustration: Dennis Yip
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.
Riding a two-year artificial intelligence boom, China’s domestic memory chipmakers have grown faster and bolder than ever – but early signs of a market cool-down threaten to test their momentum.
China’s two biggest champions in memory chip self-sufficiency, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), have leveraged state backing, new factories and advancing technology to gain market share despite US export curbs.
That rapid expansion is colliding with a shifting market.
After two years of extraordinary windfalls – which saw South Korean rivals SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics post third-quarter operating profits up more than sevenfold and nearly ninefold year on year, respectively – NAND flash contract prices are projected to flatten or fall up to 5 per cent early next year, with broader declines starting in the second quarter, according to TrendForce.
Chinese suppliers do not need to flood overseas markets to create that pressureLaila Khawaja, research director at Gavekal
Analysts say China’s rising output will increasingly complicate global supply and pricing even if its firms currently trail foreign incumbents.
Chinese and non-Chinese markets were expected to diverge in supply chains and technology paths, with Chinese suppliers’ domestic gains spilling over into global pricing and bargaining power, according to Laila Khawaja, research director at Gavekal Technologies.
“Chinese suppliers do not need to flood overseas markets to create that pressure,” she said.
China’s memory ascent
Hefei-based CXMT, founded in 2016, has become the world’s fourth-largest producer of DRAM, the working memory used in computers and smartphones. Its share of global DRAM revenue reached 9 per cent in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5 per cent a year earlier, Counterpoint Research data shows.
The CXMT logo appears on the facade of company’s production facility in Beijing, on July 29, 2026. Photo: Reuters
Government funding helped finance its entry into the capital-intensive industry. The memory boom is now funding its ramp-up: revenue rose more than eightfold to 269 billion yuan in the first nine months of 2026. Its blockbuster Shanghai initial public offering (IPO) in July raised 66.6 billion yuan, the biggest in Asia of the year.
Morgan Stanley estimates that CXMT’s monthly wafer-processing capacity could reach 500,000 by 2028, roughly 15 per cent of the global DRAM total.
CXMT is also climbing the technology ladder. It said it has begun mass production on its fifth-generation process, which produces at least 50 per cent more chips per wafer than its predecessor.
CXMT also said it had validated prototypes and would soon ship customer samples of its sixth-generation 4F2 design – a structure that enabled higher storage density by fitting more cells onto a single chip.
Wuhan-based YMTC, also founded in 2016, has made similar strides in NAND flash, which retains data without power. It ranked third globally by second-quarter shipment volume with a 16.5 per cent share, ahead of Japan’s Kioxia, Counterpoint said. Senior analyst Choi Jeong-ku expected YMTC’s 2026 revenue to grow six times faster than the broader industry.
Its strength lies partly in Xtacking, an architecture bonding memory cells and control circuitry on separate wafers for denser storage and faster data transfer. Samsung has licensed YMTC’s hybrid-bonding patents and SK Hynix has held talks about doing the same, according to local media outlets. US memory chip giant Micron Technology is facing YMTC patent lawsuits.
YMTC is seeking 33 billion yuan through a Shanghai IPO but it has not given a clear timeline yet. The company reported a first-quarter net profit of 33.4 billion yuan – more than twice its 2025 total – according to its prospectus.
Harder part
While CXMT’s 4F2 progress has fuelled local hopes of stronger Chinese offerings in DRAM, rivals were more circumspect. SK Hynix said it would keep extending its proven 6F2 architecture, noting “the timing of technological development and the timing of commercialisation are distinct”, while Micron Technology has excluded 4F2 from its road map given doubts the approach can significantly boost memory density given limits imposed by capacitor size and spacing.
Nomura expects CXMT’s 4F2 chips to reach volume production only in 2027-28, and estimates that its manufacturing technology still trails the leaders by at least three years.
Manufacturing economics show a similar gap. Macquarie equity analyst Daniel Kim estimated that CXMT’s conventional DRAM process delivered about 65 per cent as much memory per wafer as leading rivals, about two generations behind.
The divide is wider in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which stacks DRAM chips to feed AI processors. “CXMT remains primarily a conventional DRAM maker, and is not yet capable of mass-producing HBM profitably,” Khawaja said, estimating yields still trail the 85 to 90 per cent industry standard.
The YMTC logo and a computer motherboard are seen in this illustration taken April 14, 2026. Photo: Reuters
YMTC is closer to industry leaders in NAND, trailing by about a generation in layer counts, but adding layers requires advanced etching tools which are not available from local Chinese suppliers. Beyond know-how and talent, domestic toolmakers face “patent walls, not to mention the rigorous validation period required and the high requirement for tool stability,” Khawaja said.
Disruption starts at home
The immediate opportunity for Chinese memory makers was to displace foreign suppliers in the country’s smartphone, PC and storage markets, Khawaja said, adding that Beijing’s localisation push and concerns over geopolitical supply risks were encouraging buyers to consider domestic chips.
As incumbents prioritise memory for AI chips, shortages are prompting overseas buyers to qualify Chinese alternatives as second or third sources, which “could affect the big three’s [Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron Technology] bargaining power over the long run”, according to Khawaja.
While CXMT poses a more immediate challenge to the big three in conventional DRAM, YMTC’s push into enterprise SSDs could bring it closer to Samsung in data centre storage.
Counterpoint expects server products to generate nearly 39 per cent of YMTC’s revenue by 2028, up from virtually nothing in 2024, though research director MS Hwang noted the key test was winning design orders outside China.
The greater medium-term risk is an AI demand slowdown after new capacity comes online, pushing incumbents back into conventional DRAM where stronger Chinese rivals could erode pricing power, Khawaja said.
For memory makers, prosperity usually carries an expiry date: rising prices finance new factories, creating a glut that destroys profits. AI has interrupted that cycle, with SK Hynix expecting demand to outstrip supply through 2030.
By Wency Chen

title_en: North Korea seeks power for security, not supremacy, Kim says
content_en:
The North Korean leader personally welcomed new ambassadors in a rare departure from protocol after snubbing Trump’s overtures.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un addresses newly appointed ambassadors in Pyongyang in a photo released on Monday. Photo: KCNA / Reuters
Kim Jong-un said North Korea would strive to achieve “power and capability” to ensure its security and peace but would not pursue supremacy, state media reported on Monday.
Kim made the remarks at a ceremony to receive credentials from newly appointed ambassadors – including Russia’s – in a rare departure from protocol, as the task has traditionally been performed by a senior official rather than Kim himself.
The ceremony followed Kim’s snubbing of US President Donald Trump’s overtures last week during Trump’s visit to China for the Apec summit. Trump left Asia late on Thursday after a landmark trilateral summit with the Chinese and Russian presidents, without meeting Kim, as Trump had suggested he might.
“The world is now witnessing an unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Kim said at the event, according to the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), without elaborating. “The present international situation is bringing about a significant change in our understanding of national sovereignty and security.”
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un takes part in an event to receive credentials from newly appointed ambassadors in Pyongyang in a photo released on Monday. Photo: KCNA / Reuters
Pyongyang’s diplomatic goal was to “expand and develop foreign relations under the ideals of independence, peace and friendship on the principle of defending the national sovereignty and security”, he added.
“The DPRK neither pursues supremacy nor expansion,” he said, using the initials of the North’s official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed Kim – dressed in a formal suit and tie – receiving credentials, with Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui standing beside him. They also showed Kim delivering remarks and posing for photographs with each diplomat.
Kim and Trump’s previous summits during the US president’s first term sought to curb Pyongyang’s nuclear programme but yielded no concrete deal.
Despite years of UN sanctions, the North has pressed ahead with its nuclear programme, enshrining its nuclear status in law and declaring its arsenal permanent and irreversible. It has also cemented its ties with Russia by deploying troops to aid Moscow’s war effort against Ukraine.

title_en: China’s biogas tech turns Argentina’s farm waste into clean energy
content_en:
China has the patents and Argentina has the farm waste. Now the two are launching a hub to bring low-cost biogas reactors to South America.
Agriculture is a key driver of Argentina’s economy, generating vast amounts of farm waste. Photo: Shutterstock
China holds nearly 70 per cent of the world’s patents for turning farm waste into energy and useful by-products – a research stockpile born from domestic pressure to manage billions of tonnes of crop straw and manure.
Now Beijing is putting that intellectual property to work in Latin America. This year, a long-running partnership between China’s state biogas institute and Argentina’s national agricultural agency enters a new three-year phase, establishing a technology-transfer hub, developing low-cost biogas reactors for small farmers and laying the groundwork for a broader regional roll-out.
The initiative brings together the Biogas Institute of China’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs and Argentina’s National Institute of Agricultural Technology (INTA). The collaboration began with a two-month training programme in Chengdu in 2018 and was formalised in a 2019 memorandum of understanding. It was renewed in 2024 and is now expanding into a technology-transfer hub.
“One of the objectives is to introduce Chinese technology for the development of biogas production reactors, or local production using their low-cost model, focused on small-scale producers and cooperatives,” said Maria Eugenia Beily, a researcher at INTA’s Institute of Agricultural Microbiology and Zoology.
Under the new three-year phase, the Chinese and Argentine teams will test and adapt the technology to local farming conditions.
The process uses anaerobic digestion to break down crop and livestock waste into biogas, a form of clean energy that can be used directly for power or purified into biomethane for gas grids or vehicle fuel.
Instead of letting rotting farm waste release by-products and methane into the atmosphere and pollute soil and waterways, the reactors convert this gas into clean energy to replace fossil fuels. “We are generating energy from a waste,” Beily said.

title_en: India’s tech talent meets Singapore’s capital: match made in AI heaven?
content_en:
A growing partnership with Singapore could give India the push it needs to become the next AI industry leader, analysts say.
Visitors walk past a display during the Bengaluru Tech Summit in India on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
India may struggle to catch up with the FUS and China in the race to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, but analysts say its growing partnership with Singapore could offer it another path to becoming a major AI player.
By combining India’s vast software talent pool and domestic market with Singapore’s capital and hardware ecosystem, the two could develop a model for building and exporting AI technology to rival industry leaders.
One sign of the deepening cooperation came in June, when India’s Tata Communications launched a project to build a subsea cable connecting tech hubs Mumbai and Chennai with Singapore, aimed at meeting the growing AI needs of enterprises across Asia.
“We are strengthening the reliability, scalability and performance of connectivity solutions for our customers across one of the world’s busiest digital corridors,” Tata Communications said in a statement.
Despite its software prowess and engineering talent, India currently lacks the computing infrastructure and investment needed to turn its AI ambitions into globally competitive businesses.
A worker walks past workstations at a semiconductor factory in India. Photo: DigiTimes
“India generates nearly one-fifth of the world’s data and possesses a phenomenal engineering talent pool, but raw talent needs infrastructure to thrive,” said Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based adviser to governments on blockchain and information technology.
“Singapore offers exactly what India requires to monetise this human capital” – such as advanced capital markets, robust regulatory frameworks and global connectivity.
Two years ago, New Delhi launched a US$1.25 billion “IndiaAI Mission” to nurture start-ups and build infrastructure, including establishing three AI education centres focused on research.
Indian talent can plug into Singapore’s digital economy ecosystem to build and export AI solutions on a global scale, Lian said. Already, Singapore has been drawing top AI and tech talent from India, contributing to a significant cross-border talent flow.
India, which has been widely credited with successfully rolling out digital platforms for public services, aims to use them to scale up AI businesses. These efforts are being recognised in Southeast Asia.
The country is expected to play a major role in an AI push by Singaporean state-owned multinational investment firm Temasek, according to Ravi Lambah, Temasek’s India head. “AI is an interesting play for us globally. In India specifically, we see the opportunity at the application layer where India is likely to see competitive advantages … India has got this huge talent pool and the whole services ecosystem.”
Education potential
Jenny Zheng, president of Redecentralise, a South Korean not-for-profit organisation, said the synergy between the two countries was creating “a direct pipeline from Singaporean boardrooms to Indian tech parks”.
The benefits of an India-Singapore collaboration in AI extended well beyond business, she said. “We also see deep academic and corporate ties, like IIT [Indian Institute of Technology] Madras partnering with Singapore’s NUS [National University of Singapore] to build joint AI research labs.”
Singaporean exchanges and Indian tech giants also often collaborated to build cross-border payment rails, she added.
[embedded media]
As India’s tech and IT sectors shift from a traditional engineer-hour outsourcing model towards AI-driven and value-based enterprises, Indian start-ups could use Singapore as a platform to train and upskill their talent for global AI products, according to Zheng.
“Essentially, Singapore acts as the premium packaging and distribution hub. Indian talent learns to build AI products that meet global regulatory standards, transforming them from back-end coders into high-value global tech founders and asset creators,” she said.
However, the potential opportunities face barriers such as fragmented data and AI regulations, she said, adding that India’s strict data localisation laws could clash with Singapore’s model. India enforces sector-specific data localisation rules, although it does not require general personal data to stay in the country.
Another hurdle is talent mobility – as visa friction prevents the free movement of engineers needed for hands-on collaboration. Both governments needed a “bilateral AI data bridge agreement” to help data sharing for research as well as fast track “special tech visas”, she said.
Southeast Asian expansion
Zheng also saw potential for the cooperation to expand beyond Singapore into Southeast Asian countries such as Indonesia, where India is already exporting and sharing its digital public infrastructure, and Vietnam, which has been rapidly growing in hardware manufacturing. Malaysia is also positioning itself as a regional data centre hub.
An Asean-India Action Plan for 2026-2030 prioritises AI and semiconductors. In January, an Asean-India Digital Ministers’ pledged to deepen cooperation and reaffirmed their shared commitment to developing the digital domain.
Melody Chan, general partner at investment fund Arkroots, said the meeting endorsed practical AI cooperation on capacity building, standards and case studies. India-Malaysia round tables are currently exploring start-up and talent collaboration, and Indian universities are seeking partners in Vietnam for AI and quantum computing, according to Chan.
People visit the Bengaluru Tech Summit at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre in India on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
Raj Kapoor, chairman of India Blockchain Alliance, said that even though India ranked second globally with a strong pool of authors and inventors, the country faced a significant problem of brain drain as researchers and founders moved to the US for capital and customers.
To ensure that its talent stays at home, India needs capital – and this is where Singapore comes in. The city state consistently ranks as the biggest source of foreign direct investment equity capital for India.
“The next step is to direct a share of that capital into Indian AI venture and growth funds, rather than mainly into property and infrastructure. That will change the dynamics,” Kapoor said.
Singapore has another role to play too, according to Kapoor. “Singapore can also serve as a trusted test bed for Indian products headed abroad. A product that has been proven in Singapore is easier to sell to global banks, health systems and governments.”

title_en: Nvidia scandal a test of America’s respect for the rule of law
content_en:
Readers call for adherence to evidence and due process to establish guilt, and discuss Hong Kong’s competitive edge in the global battery market.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang arrives for a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington DC, on December 3. Photo: Reuters
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
America’s economic power has long rested on a remarkably simple proposition: build a business, compete freely, obey the law, and the government will protect the rules and let the open economy and free market decide.
The extraordinary events surrounding Nvidia and its founder Jensen Huang make one wonder whether that proposition still holds.
Within days, allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, escalated into a national-security controversy. US intelligence reportedly suspected her of links to Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and, importantly, no charges have yet been filed.
After Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on November 8, Nvidia announced an independent investigation and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. Days later, when reports emerged that Huang had also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, calls for him to step down grew. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO and left the board on November 12.
Of course, physically diverting restricted Nvidia chips into China could violate US export controls. But before the US moved to tighten the rules on November 16, providing Chinese companies with remote access to computing capacity located in Southeast Asia was not prohibited.
Free markets depend not only on competition but also on regulatory certainty and stability: businesses need to know the rules before they transact.
America became America because entrepreneurs could build companies, property rights mattered, government officials including the president were constrained by law, markets allocated capital, and guilt was determined through evidence and due process.
National security unquestionably matters. Wrongdoing, if established, must have consequences. But an investigation is not conviction, suspicion is not guilt, and political pressure is not the rule of law.
America’s greatest competitive advantage is not ultimately Nvidia’s chips nor artificial intelligence. It is the system that allowed Nvidia to exist in the first place. The question is whether America will sustain that system.
Stephanie YK Hasancebi, Sham Tseng
How Hong Kong can unlock battery market potential
With 76 per cent of the global battery energy storage system market and home to eight of the top 10 integrators in the world, mainland China has unrivalled expertise and manufacturing scale. Hong Kong gains little from trying to replicate it. The bigger opportunity lies beyond the factory, with the testing, financing, certification and commercialisation that turn Chinese and global new energy technologies into products trusted and adopted worldwide.
As intermittent solar and wind expand further, storage assumes critical importance for a clean energy future. Hong Kong is uniquely positioned to bring these solutions to the world stage.
A recent Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation’s (HKSTP) research report on the city’s battery energy storage development highlights how Hong Kong’s battery ecosystem is connecting key parts of the value chain that are often fragmented. Proximity to leading new energy companies and experts in the Chinese mainland sits alongside international capital, professional services and a distinct regulatory environment, creating a potential pathway from research and production to financing, certification and global deployment.
Much like London’s rise as the undisputed global centre for maritime and speciality insurance through expertise in understanding and underwriting the risks, Hong Kong’s battery opportunity could follow a similar logic. Value need not come from making the technology, but from making it easier to finance, validate and take to market.
Our study proves this is already occurring. Around 100 battery energy storage-related companies at the Science Park have been identified, while a further 60 per cent growth over the next five years is projected. The research and development operations of world leaders CATL, BYD and Gotion High-Tech are already part of this ecosystem. Hong Kong-born pioneers have joined the movement too.
To build further trust and adoption for battery energy storage system innovators worldwide, Hong Kong should take further steps to establish open trial zones for battery-storage technologies and clearer pathways for certification and cross-boundary collaboration. The objective should be to make it easier for promising technologies to move from laboratory to commercial deployment.
Terry Wong, CEO, Hong Kong Science & Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP)

title_en: Chinese state media hits out at ‘deflation trap’ warnings, defends economic performance
content_en:
A new People’s Daily commentary comes as tensions over China’s export machine mount and some economists take a cautious assessment of growth prospects.
Workers on a Jiangxi Jiangling Group Electric Vehicle production line in Nanchang, east China’s Jiangxi province, on November 9. Photo: Xinhua
The Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily has pushed back against Western descriptions of China’s economy, including claims of a “deflation trap” and “China Shock 2.0”, accusing critics of seeking to undermine confidence in the country and justify trade restrictions.
The remarks came as some economists forecast that China’s full-year growth would register near the lower end of Beijing’s official 4.5 to 5 per cent target range this year. They also cautioned that growth could slow further next year amid weak domestic demand and expectations that export momentum would fade.
“Those who talk down China’s economy will ultimately be proved wrong,” the newspaper said. It argued that some overseas media outlets and institutions had portrayed the country’s growth as unsustainable or claimed that its manufacturing strength threatened industries worldwide.
The paper cited a recent Washington Post report, which it said had selectively highlighted property-price fluctuations and weak consumer confidence to paint a bleak economic outlook.
The commentary, published on Saturday, also accused some Western politicians of invoking the “China shock” threat to deflect attention from domestic industrial problems and build support for tariffs and other trade barriers.
In defending the economy’s performance, the newspaper pointed to gross domestic product growth of 4.6 per cent in the first three quarters and a 20 per cent increase in goods traded in the first 10 months. Imports rose 23.6 per cent over the same period.
[embedded media]
Exports also remained strong, with shipments of higher-value-added products including automobiles maintaining momentum, according to a separate People’s Daily report on Sunday.
That report cited data from the State Information Centre, affiliated with the National Development and Reform Commission, and noted that cargo tonnage departing major ports rose 59.1 per cent year on year. Tonnage carried by roll-on/roll-off vessels, commonly used to transport vehicles, jumped 138.4 per cent.
The Saturday commentary nevertheless acknowledged persistent challenges, including weakness in the property market, subdued consumer confidence and difficulties upgrading traditional industries. “We have never shied away from problems,” it said.
A national conference in September stressed President Xi Jinping’s call to expand advanced manufacturing and boost self-reliance in industrial supply chains to “reinforce the foundations of the real economy”, according to a separate People’s Daily report on Monday.
Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said accusations of a “deflation trap” and “China Shock 2.0” pointed to relatively weak domestic demand, but argued those narratives could prove temporary.
“We recognise that this is a necessary cost of China’s economic transition, given that the old local government-driven growth model was unsustainable,” he said.
[embedded media]
Xing cautioned, however, that the transition would take time and that its timeline remained unclear.
S&P Global Ratings separately projected that domestic demand would remain weak in 2027. “With strong export growth helping the government meet this year’s growth target, we expect it to keep stimulus at a minimum and forecast some GDP slowdown in 2027,” the ratings agency said in a Monday report.
Morgan Stanley forecast earlier that China’s economy would grow 4.6 per cent in 2026, before slowing to 4.4 per cent in 2027. The bank expects the economy to remain in a “K-shaped” transition, where some sectors perform strongly while others struggle. Strong exports, it said, would allow policymakers to maintain fiscal restraint despite weak domestic consumption.
Even so, 2027 “should lay the foundations for broader reflation”, Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a note last week, projecting a gradual recovery in prices from 2028.
UBS Securities expects China’s annual economic growth to hold steady at about 4.6 per cent in 2027, broadly unchanged from 2026. It expects exports to contribute less as demand linked to the global energy transition fades and trade tensions persist.
This could encourage Beijing to step up domestic stimulus, including higher levels of investment in the “six networks” – an initiative to upgrade the water, electricity, computing, telecommunications, logistics and underground pipe systems by 2030 – as well as in the artificial intelligence supply chain, it said.

“Those who talk down China’s economy will ultimately be proved wrong,” the newspaper said. It argued that some overseas media outlets and institutions had portrayed the country’s growth as unsustainable or claimed that its manufacturing strength threatened industries worldwide.
The paper cited a recent Washington Post report, which it said had selectively highlighted property-price fluctuations and weak consumer confidence to paint a bleak economic outlook.
The commentary, published on Saturday, also accused some Western politicians of invoking the “China shock” threat to deflect attention from domestic industrial problems and build support for tariffs and other trade barriers.
In defending the economy’s performance, the newspaper pointed to gross domestic product growth of 4.6 per cent in the first three quarters and a 20 per cent increase in goods traded in the first 10 months. Imports rose 23.6 per cent over the same period.
[embedded media]
Exports also remained strong, with shipments of higher-value-added products including automobiles maintaining momentum, according to a separate People’s Daily report on Sunday.
That report cited data from the State Information Centre, affiliated with the National Development and Reform Commission, and noted that cargo tonnage departing major ports rose 59.1 per cent year on year. Tonnage carried by roll-on/roll-off vessels, commonly used to transport vehicles, jumped 138.4 per cent.
The Saturday commentary nevertheless acknowledged persistent challenges, including weakness in the property market, subdued consumer confidence and difficulties upgrading traditional industries. “We have never shied away from problems,” it said.
A national conference in September stressed President Xi Jinping’s call to expand advanced manufacturing and boost self-reliance in industrial supply chains to “reinforce the foundations of the real economy”, according to a separate People’s Daily report on Monday.
Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said accusations of a “deflation trap” and “China Shock 2.0” pointed to relatively weak domestic demand, but argued those narratives could prove temporary.
“We recognise that this is a necessary cost of China’s economic transition, given that the old local government-driven growth model was unsustainable,” he said.
[embedded media]
Xing cautioned, however, that the transition would take time and that its timeline remained unclear.
S&P Global Ratings separately projected that domestic demand would remain weak in 2027. “With strong export growth helping the government meet this year’s growth target, we expect it to keep stimulus at a minimum and forecast some GDP slowdown in 2027,” the ratings agency said in a Monday report.
Morgan Stanley forecast earlier that China’s economy would grow 4.6 per cent in 2026, before slowing to 4.4 per cent in 2027. The bank expects the economy to remain in a “K-shaped” transition, where some sectors perform strongly while others struggle. Strong exports, it said, would allow policymakers to maintain fiscal restraint despite weak domestic consumption.
Even so, 2027 “should lay the foundations for broader reflation”, Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a note last week, projecting a gradual recovery in prices from 2028.
UBS Securities expects China’s annual economic growth to hold steady at about 4.6 per cent in 2027, broadly unchanged from 2026. It expects exports to contribute less as demand linked to the global energy transition fades and trade tensions persist.
This could encourage Beijing to step up domestic stimulus, including higher levels of investment in the “six networks” – an initiative to upgrade the water, electricity, computing, telecommunications, logistics and underground pipe systems by 2030 – as well as in the artificial intelligence supply chain, it said.

title_en: As brain-computer interface boom enters next phase, China pushes to shape global standards
content_en:
Crowded sector sees growing number of challengers to Elon Musk’s Neuralink.
A user tries on a brain-computer interface device at a robot conference in Beijing. Photo: People’s Daily Online
China will set up a new standard-setting task force for brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, while a state-backed think tank has urged investors to remain patient as the nascent but increasingly crowded sector develops.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said it would create the new working group under its BCI standardisation technical committee at an industry conference this week, state-backed news outlet Securities Times reported.
The ministry would host a BCI “Standards Week” event in Wuhan on Wednesday and Thursday, where industry participants and government agencies could “work closely” to advance the practical application of BCI standards, the committee said earlier this month.
The move comes as China ramps up efforts to shape standards for the emerging sector, which Beijing identified as one of six “industries of the future” in its 15th five-year plan.
Last month, the country became chair of a BCI subcommittee jointly overseen by the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, two of the world’s leading standards bodies.
BCI devices translate neural signals into commands for external devices and are designed to help restore speech or mobility. The technology has drawn growing interest as an increasing number of Chinese firms seek to challenge Neuralink, the world’s leading BCI firm, co-founded by SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
China was now home to more than 250 BCI firms, with more than 77 per cent concentrated in three major urban clusters: Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, the Yangtze River Delta, and the Greater Bay Area, according to state-backed news outlet Beijing Daily in a report on Sunday.
The report cited new research by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, a think tank under the information technology ministry, that had yet to be released publicly.
According to the academy, the global BCI industry was expanding rapidly, with the number of companies worldwide increasing to 1,175 this year from more than 800 last year.
The think tank reportedly said China’s BCI sector would likely enter a phase of consolidation and tighter regulation, with companies developing similar products moving into specific markets.
It also warned that the sector’s payment models and talent pools remained underdeveloped, and said investors would need to “remain patient” as the industry matured.
Continued policy support for BCI firms would also be necessary, it added.
By Xinmei Shen

title_en: How will China’s ties with Myanmar change with the ICJ’s genocide ruling?
content_en:
The ruling could complicate Beijing’s relationship with the country and could affect infrastructure projects, observers say.
Myanmar’s Union Minister for the Ministry of the President’s Office Ko Ko Hlaing sits in the courtroom as the International Court of Justice delivers its judgment in the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, on November 19. Photo: Reuters
An international court ruling of genocide against Myanmar might complicate Beijing’s diplomatic engagement with Naypyidaw and cast a shadow over Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure projects in the country, observers warn.
The landmark decision by the UN’s highest judicial body covers Myanmar’s 2017 military campaign against the majority-Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state that killed at least 10,000 people and forced hundreds of thousands more to flee.
The decision handed down on Thursday is the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has held a state responsible for genocide in its 81-year history, and was passed by a 9-6 vote with Chinese judge Xue Hanqin dissenting.
While the ruling is final and legally binding, the court has no enforcement powers.
The decision comes as institutions of international justice are under pressure. Just hours before it was announced, the leaders of China, the US and Russia agreed at a summit to work together to constrain the International Criminal Court system, which they said “must not abuse [its] jurisdiction”. While the ICJ is a UN body, the International Criminal Court is a separate, independent court.
In response to the verdict, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Friday there was “very complex historical, ethnic and religious background” behind the Rohingya crisis and that Beijing was willing to play “a constructive role” to facilitate dialogue among different parties.
[embedded media]
When asked if Xue dissented on Beijing’s instruction, Guo said the judge was serving “independently in her personal capacity”.
He said international courts should exercise their powers prudently and in accordance with the law. “China has concerns over issues such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” Guo said.
While the ruling is widely seen as a legal blow to the new government led by former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing – who was sworn in in May following an election that several Western countries condemned as a sham – observers said the verdict was unlikely to derail ties between China and its strategically important neighbour, given Beijing’s long-standing policy of non-interference.
Yin Yihang, a Myanmar affairs expert and research fellow at Yunnan Academy of Social Sciences, said Xue’s vote aligned with Beijing’s consistent position on state sovereignty and opposition to the politicisation of human rights.
“The ruling targets the events from 2017 and did not directly involve Chinese-funded projects or personnel in Myanmar,” Yin said, noting that Beijing maintains the issue should be handled within Myanmar’s domestic reconciliation framework.
“Beijing is unlikely to publicly condemn the Myanmar government, endorse the ruling or alter its principle of non-interference.”
However, Yin warned that China’s ties with the country might come under extra scrutiny after the ruling, as its engagement with the Min Aung Hlaing government could be cast as Beijing backing a “convicted regime”.
The ruling was also expected to cast a shadow over investment in Myanmar, Yin said.
Should Western powers impose fresh sanctions on Myanmar based on the verdict, Chinese investments could face secondary sanctions and heightened compliance scrutiny, he added.
[embedded media]
That may include flagship Belt and Road Initiative projects in Rakhine, including the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port, China-Myanmar oil and gas pipelines and parts of a planned railway linking China’s Yunnan province with the Bay of Bengal.
“The verdict will not alter realities on the ground, but it may prolong international scrutiny and uncertainty over Rakhine, affecting the pace at which these projects are implemented.”
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and the director of the China programme at the Washington-based Stimson Centre, agreed that the verdict was unlikely to trigger immediate shifts on the ground, noting that the ICJ had limited power to enforce its ruling.
She added that the recent resumption of Myanmar’s engagement with the United States might add a new layer of complexity for Beijing’s handling of its ties with Naypyidaw.
“China is currently having some issues in its relationship with Myanmar so I don’t think Beijing will be inclined to come out publicly to say much at the moment,” she said.
On Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing confirmed that direct talks were ongoing with the US. Reuters reported in October that Michael Vance, the US assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, met Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw in September.
In the long run, the ruling could pose a distinct dilemma for Beijing as it has to remain deeply involved in Myanmar to protect its economic and broader security interests, according to Peng Xu, a research fellow at the University of Manchester’s Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute.
[embedded media]
While international courts have previously recognised genocides in Rwanda, Bosnia and Cambodia, those rulings convicted individuals rather than states, so this ruling poses a new challenge to China’s foreign policy.
“China has shown in the past that international judicial accountability does not necessarily stop it from working with sanctioned or accused governments,” Peng said.
“But when the ICJ explicitly rules that a strategic partner has committed genocide, it raises a fundamental question: can China continue the existing non-interference logic?”
By Laura Zhou

title_en: BYD pledges to fight EU sales ban in infringement battle with Jaguar Land Rover
content_en:
Chinese firm vows to pursue ‘every legal avenue’ after ruling says Fang Cheng Bao Ti7 infringes on design of JLR’s Defender model.
BYD’s Ti 7 SUV, also known as the Titan 7. Photo: Handout
Chinese electric vehicle (EV) giant BYD will appeal a sales ban on one of its premium SUVs after a Dutch court ruled that it infringed on the design of the Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) Defender.
“BYD strongly disagrees with the judgment and will appeal it,” the Chinese carmaker said in a statement. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights. We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.”
The statement came after the District Court of The Hague issued an injunction on Friday, which bars BYD from selling its Fang Cheng Bao Ti7 electric SUV in the European Union.
“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” the court said in the ruling. “The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”
The court also put a temporary ban on production of the SUV at BYD’s new plant in Hungary, though the factory had yet to begin assembling it.
“The legal dispute between BYD and JLR will be closely monitored by other Chinese automotive groups, as all of them aim to launch more new models abroad to increase their overseas sales,” said Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service consultancy. “Chinese carmakers need to pay more attention to legal risks as they expand abroad.”
In August, court-ordered bailiffs raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands to seize paper and digital documents about the design of the Ti7, after JLR took the Chinese electric car assembler to court over copycat claims, according to the Times of London.
JLR alleged that BYD could have infringed upon its IP rights by reverse-engineering its Defender vehicle, which is the luxury carmaker’s most popular model with global sales of over 100,000 units in 2025.
Chinese carmakers need to pay more attention to legal risks as they expand abroadChen Jinzhu, Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service
On November 12, JLR was ordered by the District Court of The Hague to destroy documents obtained in the raids of BYD’s offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp.
Fang Cheng Bao is a premium brand launched by BYD in 2023, a challenge to the likes of Toyota’s Prado and Land Rover amid the domestic market’s rapid shift to battery cars.
BYD, the largest carmaker in mainland China, sold more than 1.51 million vehicles abroad in the first 10 months of 2026, up 93.8 per cent on year, according to its own sales data.
Nick Lai, head of auto research in Asia-Pacific at JPMorgan, forecast in May that Chinese carmakers led by BYD were expected to deliver 2.5 million cars to ­customers in western European countries including Germany, Italy, France and the UK in 2028, a surge of 150 per cent from about 1 million units last year.
By Daniel Ren

title_en: India to test all bottled water brands after Bisleri sample found unsafe
content_en:
The home-grown brand competes with PepsiCo’s Aquafina and Coca-Cola’s Kinley in India’s US$3.6 billion packaged drinking water market.
Bisleri packaged drinking water bottles are stacked inside a shop in Kolkata, India, on March 12. Photo: Reuters
India’s food safety regulator has found a sample of Bisleri International’s packaged drinking water ‌unsafe in a major setback for the country’s biggest and best-known bottled water brand, and a government source said samples from all companies would now be tested.
In light of the findings, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India planned to test more Bisleri samples from across the nation, as well as those of other companies, a government source said on Monday.
Bisleri competes with PepsiCo’s Aquafina and Coca-Cola’s Kinley in India’s packaged drinking water market, valued at US$3.6 billion in ⁠2025, according to Persistence Market Research.
“Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls,” Bisleri said, ‌adding it will cooperate with the regulators. The brand, introduced in India in 1965, is a household name in the country where poor water quality often prompts people and tourists ‌to buy packaged water both for homes and at restaurants.
A second government source said the batches linked ⁠to the unsafe sample had ⁠been recalled, and subsequent testing of products showed no issues with water quality.
A man drinks water from a tap on the outskirts of Jammu, India, on May 19. The country’s poor water quality often prompts people and tourists ‌to buy packaged water both for homes and at restaurants. Photo: AP
The sample, collected from Bisleri’s premises, did not meet prescribed limits on bromate, ‌a chemical formed as a by-product of certain disinfection processes, the food safety authority said in a social media post on Sunday. After Bisleri appealed the finding, the government regulator still ‌found ‌the sample unsafe but instead said it had detected polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs.
PAHs are of ‌serious public health concern due to their toxic, mutagenic and carcinogenic properties, according to research published last year on the National ⁠Library of Medicine’s PubMed database.
Some individuals who ingested high concentrations of bromate experienced kidney problems and hearing loss, according to the ⁠New York health department, though they were exposed to levels many thousands of times higher than the drinking water standard.
Bisleri said in its statement that the sample collected from its Goa facility last year showed bromate ‌levels of 12mcg per litre ‌against the prescribed limit of 10mcg per litre, but further independent testing arranged by the company showed the chemical was within prescribed limits.
India’s food regulator has stepped up enforcement against major brands this year, including legal action against Nestle over a baby food sample it found substandard in September.
By Reuters

title_en: China sentences ministry official to death for leaking over 100 state secrets
content_en:
Beijing’s secrecy watchdog outlines how foreign operatives used money and blackmail to turn a ministry cadre into a double agent.
A social media account related to China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection warns Chinese to beware of being manipulated or honey-trapped after a ministry official was sentenced to death. Photo: Shutterstock
A Chinese ministry official has been sentenced to death for spying after being groomed and blackmailed into handing over dozens of state secrets to a foreign intelligence agency, according to a rare public disclosure by Beijing’s state secrecy apparatus.
The official, identified only by his surname, Ma, was convicted of espionage, stripped of his political rights for life and all his personal property was confiscated, according to an account published on Monday by Baomiguan, a social media channel of Jincheng Press, a publishing arm of the National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The report did not disclose when the trial or sentencing took place, which court issued the verdict or whether the sentence had been carried out. Nor did it identify the government ministry Ma worked for or the foreign countries involved, referring to them only as Country A and Country B.
[embedded media]
Public disclosures of death sentences in espionage cases are relatively rare in China, where judicial proceedings involving national security are typically conducted behind closed doors.
According to the account, Ma’s recruitment began while he was posted overseas in Country A, where he became acquainted with an intelligence officer from Country B identified by the Chinese transliteration “Kailin”.
Kailin frequently invited Ma to meet under the pretext of improving communication and learning Chinese, offering modest payments in exchange for regular contacts. Over time, their discussions shifted towards politically sensitive topics and international current affairs, before Kailin began probing Ma for details about the personnel and operations of China’s mission in Country A.
Ma subsequently leaked substantial sensitive information regarding the mission and handed over an internal telephone directory, according to the social media account.
As their contact deepened, Kailin introduced Ma to a colleague identified as “Tang Zheng”. During their meeting, Tang directly demanded that Ma formally join Country B’s intelligence service, threatening to report Ma’s “past illegal activities” to Chinese authorities if he refused.
Facing blackmail, Ma capitulated and accepted tasks assigned by Country B’s intelligence handlers. He signed a formal “cooperation agreement” that included clauses requiring “confidentiality” and “loyalty”, receiving a fixed monthly stipend and a dedicated laptop to send and receive intelligence.
Ma embarked on a “prolonged period of espionage” from inside his ministry after completing his overseas posting and returning to China, the report said. By day, he gathered classified materials accessed through his official duties according to tasks assigned by Country B; by night, he compiled the files at home and transmitted them via covert espionage websites.
The report said Ma stole and handed over more than 100 pieces of intelligence in total, of which nine were designated “secret” and 26 were “confidential” – the second and third highest tiers in China’s state secret classification system.
It said that before his arrest, he had collected more than 1 million yuan (US$150,000) in espionage-related funds through domestic drop-offs and overseas meetings, alongside performance bonuses based on the quality of the material provided.
Commenting on the case, Baomiguan warned Chinese civil servants to “clean up their social circles, living circles and friend circles” and remain vigilant against being “honey-trapped” by foreign intelligence services through “emotional manipulation, financial enticement and coercion”.
The disclosure comes amid a sustained public awareness campaign by China’s state security apparatus – including the Ministry of State Security (MSS) – warning citizens of increasingly sophisticated foreign intelligence tactics.
In previous case studies and advisories, the MSS has identified several main demographics often targeted by overseas spy agencies, including civil servants and government cadres with direct access to state secrets and internal policy documents; staff at scientific research institutes, university faculty and students – particularly those working in core technologies, cutting-edge industries or studying and visiting abroad; and individuals living or working near classified facilities and military installations.
[embedded media]
It has also repeatedly warned the public to guard against disguises used by foreign operatives to establish contact and build trust, including overseas scholars or project researchers dangling academic exchanges, surveys or assistance with publishing in international journals, as well as “caring confidants” exploiting emotional vulnerabilities among young professionals or individuals experiencing workplace and family setbacks.
Authorities have also flagged operatives posing as “friends with similar interests” in online forums and chat rooms, “wealthy businesspeople” offering lucrative investments, and fake consultancies or detective agencies recruiting locals for paid research or photography near defence facilities, alongside cover as journalists, visa officers and non-governmental organisation workers.
By William Zheng

title_en: SCMP, SEAFIC sign 3-year deal to host Asean Futurist Conference
content_en:
The one-day, exclusive by invitation-only event will gather leaders across various sectors to examine trends shaping regional competitiveness over the next decade.
SCMP publisher Tammy Tam and SEAFIC chairman Tengku Zafrul Aziz at the signing ceremony on Monday to stage the inaugural Asean Futurist Conference. Photo: Sun Yeung
The South China Morning Post and the Southeast Asian Futures Initiative Centre (SEAFIC) on Monday signed an agreement to stage the inaugural Asean Futurist Conference, set to take place on April 19 next year in Kuala Lumpur.
The one-day, exclusive by invitation-only event will gather about 150 leaders across government, business and academia to examine trends shaping regional competitiveness over the next decade.
SCMP publisher Tammy Tam and SEAFIC chairman Tengku Zafrul Aziz signed for their respective organisations, following a memorandum of understanding exchanged earlier in August in Kuala Lumpur.
Zafrul said the proposed conference programme would cover topics from artificial intelligence and digital sovereignty to workforce readiness, sustainable energy systems and food security, examining how long-term shifts should inform current policy, investment and business decisions.
SCMP publisher Tammy Tam at the signing ceremony on Monday. Photo: Sun Yeung
“I am truly delighted to mark this moment with Tengku Zafrul with the signing of a formal three-year partnership agreement,” Tam said.
“These challenges are deeply connected, and no single sector can solve them alone,” Tam said, adding that the collaboration aimed to spark “the kind of dialogue and cooperation that helps Southeast Asia build a more resilient, competitive and future-ready region”.
Zafrul said the discussions would explore possible scenarios over a five- to 10-year horizon and how governments and businesses should navigate them.
“It’s not easy to predict, but it’s important that we anticipate as many situations and be prepared for possible eventualities,” he said.
Supply chains were now being driven not just by commercial concerns, but also security and strategic considerations, Zafrul added.
Tam said the partnership combined SCMP’s journalistic reach and convening experience with SEAFIC’s research depth and strategic foresight.
“By combining our strengths, we can create a meaningful bridge between policymakers, business leaders, investors and researchers, and connect long-term thinking with the decisions that matter today,” she said.
SEAFIC chairman Tengku Zafrul Aziz at the signing ceremony on Monday. Photo: Sun Yeung
SEAFIC, a Malaysia-based think tank focused on economic development, trade, investment and international cooperation, will contribute research, thematic direction and stakeholder connections.
The organisation was also developing a decision-impact index with another institution, to support planning rather than offer definitive predictions, Zafrul said.
Beyond external disruptions, he said Southeast Asian countries must strengthen public understanding of regional cooperation, including job and market competition concerns, noting the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ relevance was less apparent on the ground than to companies.
“To realise the full potential, there needs to be more trust and harmonisation of policies so that [the] economies of scale that we always talk about when we sell Asean become a reality,” he said.
By Vincent Tan

title_en: From steel to style: China’s ‘flagship’ AI factories move beyond heavy industry
content_en:
Clothing, alcohol and electronics makers feature in the latest batch of 34 facilities recognised by Beijing.
A clothing factory run by Jiangsu-based HLA Group, where AI-powered systems are augmented alongside manual labour. Photo: Xinhua
Before a shirt reaches a shop in China, artificial intelligence may have already played a part in making it, from helping manufacturers understand consumer preferences to turning those insights into design ideas.
At a factory run by Jiangsu-based HLA Group, AI-integrated systems work alongside human operators to coordinate production. The approach is gaining ground across China’s manufacturing sector, extending from heavy industry into consumer goods.
On Thursday, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) named 34 facilities in its latest batch of “flagship” smart factories, including the one run by HLA Group. Launched in 2024, the programme aims to upgrade supply chains and encourage the use of AI and other advanced technologies.
The programme has several tiers, with flagship smart factories at the highest level. To qualify, facilities in this category are required to have an AI application rate of at least 60 per cent.
Traditional industries such as steelmaking and aerospace dominated the first batch of 15 factories, announced in late 2025. Consumer-facing manufacturers were sparse yet included home appliance makers Gree Electric and Haier.
The latest batch, however, reflects AI’s expanding reach across manufacturing. HLA Group is the first apparel maker to join the programme, joining baijiu distiller Luzhou Laojiao, pharmaceutical company Tasly and television maker Hisense. Carmakers Xiaomi, Seres and FAW-Volkswagen were also included.
AI applications accounted for more than 70 per cent of all use cases across these facilities, with more than 1,000 industrial AI agents developed and daily use of tokens exceeding 300 million, according to a Thursday press release from the World Intelligent Manufacturing Conference.
The event, co-hosted by entities including the Jiangsu provincial government and the MIIT, brought together representatives from all 34 factories.
[embedded media]
“Seeing consumer-facing manufacturers clear high AI thresholds shows that AI is no longer just a back-end automation tool,” said Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting.
“Rather, it is actively being used to connect real-time demand insights to flexible production, allowing companies to design and deliver better products at scale and respond faster to shifting consumer preferences.”
The effects are reaching beyond the factories themselves. The 34 facilities had helped nearly 4,000 other companies upgrade their operations by sharing technologies, solutions and experiences, according to the press release.
Montufar-Helu said the shift reflected Beijing’s view of AI as a foundational technology that could boost economic efficiency, strengthen technological self-reliance and improve resource allocation. This had encouraged the government to play a more active role in driving adoption across sectors, he added.
“Rather than simply waiting for market-driven adoption, the government is using top-tier factories to prove out industrial AI use cases, from optimising production and quality control to improving safety and end-to-end traceability,” Montufar-Helu said.
Beijing has repeatedly stressed the importance of applying AI in real-world settings. Speaking at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen last week, President Xi Jinping described China as “a supersized innovation testing ground where frontier technologies are tested, improved and upgraded in real-world scenarios, and are then turned into high-quality growth drivers”.
At a press conference in late October, an MIIT official also highlighted AI’s importance to developing next-generation smart manufacturing, saying it could “enhance the self-perception, decision-making and execution capabilities of equipment and systems, drive changes in production methods and business models and help manufacturers cut costs, improve efficiency and better meet diverse market demand”.
The MIIT was also developing more targeted policy measures to deepen AI integration in manufacturing, the official said.
By Alice Li

title_en: Huge planet, tiny star: discovery challenges textbook view of how giants form
content_en:
Planet nearly five times the mass of Jupiter circling small, dim star doesn’t appear to fit the widely accepted picture, astrophysicist says.
Astronomers discovered a planet nearly five times the mass of Jupiter. Image: Shutterstock
Chinese and American astronomers have found a planet nearly five times the mass of Jupiter circling a small, dim star, challenging the textbook view of how giant planets form and how many of them are out there.
The team, from Carnegie Science in Washington and Shanghai Jiao Tong and Tsinghua universities, spotted the planet – known as HIP 88962 b – with the Magellan Clay Telescope in Chile after 16 years of observations.
Its host star has only two-thirds the mass of our sun – too small to build a world this big under the leading theory that gas giants grow slowly around a rocky core, the researchers reported in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Tuesday.
Alan Boss, the paper’s lead author and an astrophysicist who studies how planets are born, said the discovery did not appear to fit the widely accepted picture.
Instead, it supports what he called a “heretical” idea: that some giants like Jupiter are not built pebble by pebble, but form almost at once when the gas around a young star collapses into clumps.
He said that if there were more than one way to make such planets, there were likely to be many more of them than expected – including in places where astronomers would not think to look.
[embedded media]
For this study, Boss said the Carnegie scientists made the telescope observations, while colleagues in China analysed satellite data that helped pin down the planet’s mass.
Scientists have for decades believed that giant planets are assembled from the bottom up, starting with a small core of rock and ice that later gathers a thick shell of gas.
But that slow route struggles around small stars, which start out with thin disks of raw material. Computer models predict such stars rarely produce gas giants, especially far from home.
HIP 88962 b defies those predictions. It orbits at about six times Earth’s distance from the sun, on a stretched, oval path unlike the rounder ones that core-built giants tend to follow. It better fits the reverse, top-down scenario Boss first proposed in 1997, the researchers wrote.
The planet turned up in a Magellan survey of nearby stars that began in 2010. It is too faint and too close to its host to be seen directly, so the astronomers used the so-called wobble method to track how its gravity rocked the star back and forth, slightly shifting the colour of its light.
Since the planet takes about 19 years to complete one orbit, the team needed well over a decade of patient watching to trace its full pattern. An earlier study with a smaller telescope in Chile had found nothing, because its observations spanned only about two years.
The discovery also matters for the search for life beyond Earth. Nasa counts the star among those that could host Earth-like planets, and the team said they had picked up a faint signal that might come from a second, much closer planet.
“We will continue to monitor HIP 88962 to search for any wobbles caused by other exoplanets in this system,” Boss said.
By Ling Xin

title_en: John Lee hails young Hongkongers’ ‘fighting spirit’ after record WorldSkills haul
content_en:
City’s largest-ever delegation of 41 participants returns with 15 accolades, the most Hong Kong has won.
Chief Executive John Lee (front row, centre) has praised Team Hong Kong for their record haul at the WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai. Photo: Sun Yeung
Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has praised the city’s younger generation for their “outstanding skills and fighting spirit” after a record-breaking performance at an international vocational competition.
Speaking at a reception on Monday, Lee also thanked the trainers of the teams that won one silver medal and 14 medals for excellence at the WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai.
The 41-strong delegation is the largest Hong Kong has ever sent to the tournament, while the 15 accolades are the most ever won at what has been dubbed the Olympics of vocational skills.
“As long as people focus on their strengths and strive for excellence, they can excel in any profession,” Lee said. “Hong Kong’s contestants have shown their outstanding skills and fighting spirit, showcasing the talent of its younger generation to the world.”
Lee also hailed the efforts of the city’s Standing Committee on Youth Skills Competition, the Vocational Training Council (VTC) and other industry bodies for the part they played in September’s success.
Vocational and professional education was “an important pillar of Hong Kong’s education system”, Lee said, adding that the city’s first five-year plan had called for its high-quality development.
“The government will continue to work with the VTC and different sectors to create more diverse opportunities for young people, enabling them to apply what they have learned and make the best use of their talents.”
Tse Yu-lok (left) received a medal for excellence in welding and Gordon Tang won a silver medal in the rail vehicle technology category. Photo: Sun Yeung
Held in mainland China for the first time, the WorldSkills Competition brought together about 1,400 contestants from nearly 70 countries and regions.
The Hong Kong delegation competed in 37 skills categories and won 15 awards across a wide range of disciplines, including concrete construction work, cybersecurity, patisserie and confectionery and autonomous mobile robotics.
Among them was Gordon Tang Kwong-tai, a technician at the MTR Corporation and a graduate of the Hong Kong Institute of Vocational Education, who won a silver medal in the rail vehicle technology category. He was also named the top scorer of the Hong Kong team.
Having spent 18 months preparing for the competition, Tang said he was delighted with the result and that his hard work “had finally been recognised”.
Tang said he hoped to continue his professional development with the ultimate goal of becoming a railway engineer.
“I hope to apply what I have learned from the competition to my daily work and continue contributing to safe and reliable railway services for Hong Kong passengers,” he said.
