title_en: Indonesia’s Prabowo names 2 vice-president candidates to replace Gibran
content_en:
The candidates are Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former foreign minister Sugiono, who is the ruling party’s secretary general.
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto speaks to journalists alongside Speaker of the People’s Consultative Assembly Ahmad Muzani in Jakarta on Monday after submitting the names of two candidates to succeed former vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka. Photo: AFP
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto put forward on Monday two candidates to succeed Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who has resigned as vice-president following a scandal over his high school diploma.
Gibran’s resignation on November 12, after a Supreme Court ruling annulled his overseas high school qualification, has added to pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, corruption and wildfires.
The former vice-president is the son of Prabowo’s predecessor and political rival Joko Widodo, whose popularity is widely seen to have helped the incumbent to the top job.
Prabowo submitted on Monday the names of two candidates for parliament to consider, speaker of the People’s Consultative Assembly Ahmad Muzani told reporters.
Lawmakers will convene on December 11 to select between Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former foreign minister Sugiono, who is the ruling party’s secretary general.
“I believe that both of them will do their best for the nation, the state and the people of Indonesia,” Prabowo told reporters.
Then Indonesian foreign minister Sugiono meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on the sidelines of a UN Security Council meeting in New York in May. Photo: Xinhua
Sugiono, who like many Indonesians uses only one name, is sometimes referred to as the president’s “ideological child” due to their close working relationship.
A vice-president from Prabowo’s party could help “secure the popularity” of the president ahead of a potential re-election bid in 2029, Centre for Strategic and International Studies researcher Dominique Nicky Fachrizal said before the nomination.
The 47-year-old Sugiono, who had a short stint in the army’s special forces unit before retiring in 2004, was made coordinating minister for human development and cultural affairs in a cabinet reshuffle last month.
Andi, 58, was a businessman before serving as the agriculture minister under Widodo, also known as Jokowi, between 2014 and 2019.
He returned to the post following a corruption scandal involving his successor and was reappointed when Prabowo came to power in 2024.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Australia to treat AI as key foreign policy challenge, warning of risks to democracy
content_en:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong is also expected to speak about the middle powers’ growing influence and the US-China strategic competition.
Australia is expected to unveil a new foreign policy stance on artificial intelligence on Tuesday. Photo: Shutterstock
Australia will treat artificial intelligence as a key challenge in ⁠its foreign policy, warning the ⁠technology was reshaping society’s foundations ⁠and giving overseas actors new ways to interfere in its democracy.
In a major address to parliament on Tuesday setting out Australia’s changing foreign policy approach, Foreign Minister Penny Wong is expected to name AI alongside forces such as the growing influence ‌of middle powers and strategic competition between the US and China.
“Technology is transforming the foundations and dimensions of economic and strategic power,” Wong will say.
“Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies are spreading and disrupting faster than any previous revolutionary technologies – reordering our lives, economies and militaries in ways we cannot fully foresee.”
It comes after the Australian government earlier this month announced it ⁠would toughen its AI regulation, mandating companies report breaches and establishing a dedicated regulator for the technology, ‌following revelations an OpenAI agent breached the database of the country’s health system.
Citing recent foreign disinformation operations, Wong will also warn in her speech, entitled “Securing Australia’s ‌future in a changing world: Australian foreign policy for a new era”, that AI ⁠tools make interference in ⁠Australia’s democracy by foreign actors faster, cheaper and harder to recognise.
“We are strengthening our critical technology, infrastructure and cyber resilience, ‌and legislating mandatory safety and security protections for every frontier AI company that operates in Australia,” Wong is expected to say.
Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong delivers a lecture at the Lowy Institute in Sydney in August. Photo: Reuters
While welcoming ‌investment ‌and innovation in frontier AI, she will say it must be “on terms that work for ‌all Australians”.
Australia intends to help shape the race to develop advanced models by ensuring it “does not reward ⁠speed over prudence”, Wong is expected to say, drawing comparisons to nuclear non-proliferation and online safety.
“Australia is working ⁠with partners on AI safety, making it a shared, global endeavour … Australia has helped shape the international order before, in non-proliferation and in online safety. With artificial intelligence, we ‌intend to do it ‌again.”
Wong will also outline five other key forces reshaping the international order.
These include changes in how the US and China define and pursue their interests, the influence of middle powers, the growing threat or use of force and coercion, and increasing difficulty in achieving collective international action.
By Reuters

title_en: Chinese youth ditch office jobs for global travel as ‘flight companions’ for seniors, pets
content_en:
Industry insiders stress it is no easy gig: job demands multiple visas, translation skills, and deep knowledge of global airport procedures.
More young people in China are quitting office jobs to work as paid “flight companions” — helping elderly travellers through customs and delivering pets or goods globally. Photo: Shutterstock
Some young people in China are turning away from traditional office jobs to “travel the world for free” as flight companions.
This autumn, a wave of job-seeking posts appeared on mainland Chinese social media, as self-described “international flight companions” sought clients.
One woman, who uses the handle “Spicy K,” wrote that she plans to draw on her fluent English and solo-travel experience to launch a flight companion service.
Her offerings include helping elderly travellers navigate customs, transporting pets and carrying goods.
She also said she refuses to leave the airport in some Southeast Asian countries where scam gangs are known to operate.
In the past, several Chinese career bloggers have promoted the role to international students as a niche career path suited to avid travellers.
One flight companion shares her top tips for making it in the gig. Photo: Douyin
Meanwhile, other social media accounts claim to offer more structured services.
An account with more than 15,000 followers, called “Wall Street Engine,” advertises “butler-style” companionship for Chinese travellers heading to Britain.
The service costs £150 (US$200) per hour, plus a £450 service fee. Staff must be men aged 35 or older, have lived in the UK for at least three years, and wear British-style suits throughout the trip.
In October, the mainland newspaper Yangtse Evening Post profiled Liu, who has worked in the industry for five years.
An avid traveller who has visited dozens of countries, Liu moved into full-time flight companionship after connecting with cross-border agencies.
He charges from several thousand to tens of thousands of yuan per trip, including round-trip airfare, meals and accommodation. His clients have ranged from three-year-old children to seniors in their 80s.
From three-year-olds to seniors in their 80s, one such companion handles everything for his clients – including entry and exit paperwork and in-flight care. Photo: Shutterstock
“People living abroad often want their elderly parents or children in China to visit during the holidays, but they don’t feel comfortable letting them fly alone,” Liu said.
For these passengers, he checks their health in advance, prepares their entry and exit paperwork, and looks after them throughout the flight.
Clients also hire Liu to transport items. One memorable “passenger” was a little girl’s bedtime doll, accidentally left behind when her family moved to the US.
His team also has pet specialists, who once escorted a dog valued at 200,000 yuan (US$30,000).
Another flight companion, surnamed Wang, from Hangzhou in eastern China, specialises in hand-carrying urgent business items such as contracts and trade show samples, offering faster delivery than standard couriers.
Transporting pets is another key service, with one specialist once escorting a dog valued at 200,000 yuan (US$30,000). Photo: Getty Images
However, industry insiders stress that the barrier to entry is high: the work requires multiple visas, translation skills and extensive knowledge of airport procedures around the world.
Liu also warned of legal risks, noting that companions must inspect cargo to avoid prohibited items. The work can also take a physical toll, with jet lag and long periods of sitting. He logged more than 1,000 flight hours last year alone.
As one online commenter cautioned, the role involves handling constant emergencies and is “not suitable for young people who just want to travel for free.”
“This job is not for idle people with nothing better to do either, because they probably would not even be able to get the visas approved,” another commenter wrote.
By Zoey Zhang

title_en: More power, more weapons: what’s next for China’s J-35A stealth fighter?
content_en:
CCTV report suggests changes will be incremental rather than all at once but experts question how soon the jet will be fully operational.
The J-35A stealth fighter is the Chinese military’s land-based variant of the carrier-borne J-35. Photo: CCTV
China’s J-35A stealth fighter could receive upgrades to its engines, weapons, electronic systems and radar evasion capabilities, according to a military commentator on state broadcaster CCTV, as Beijing continues to develop its newest land-based low-observable warplane.
Shao Yongling identified four possible improvements, including fitting the twin-engined jet with what she termed a “full version” of China’s WS-19 engine and widening the range of weapons carried internally, helping it to remain difficult to detect by radar.
The J-35A’s debut two years ago at the Zhuhai air show made China the second country after the United States to have two types of stealth fighter jets. However, questions remain about how soon it will be fully operational and what its role will be.
Some experts predict the J-35A will become a widely used multi-role workhorse alongside the heavier J-20, while others suggest the new fighter will initially focus on air-defence missions.
In the CCTV report on November 12, Shao said the J-35A – the land-based counterpart of the PLA Navy’s carrier-borne J-35 – was more likely to receive smaller upgrades over time than all at once.
These could include improvements to its electronic systems to help pilots detect stealth aircraft and reduce their workload, as well as changes to make the fighter harder to detect in different environments, she suggested.
Akhil Kadidal, senior Asia-Pacific aviation reporter at defence publication Janes, estimates that each of the WS-19 engines used in the initial production J-35As produces 98,000 newtons (10,000kg-force) of thrust.
This would be sufficient for combat manoeuvring but the possible upgrades mentioned by Shao suggested the aircraft could benefit from more power at high altitudes and with a full weapons load, he said.
Some experts predict the J-35A will become a widely used multi-role workhorse alongside the heavier J-20. Photo: AFP
If the estimates are correct, the two WS-19 engines would give the J-35A a combined thrust of nearly 196,000 newtons – in theory comparable to the roughly 191,000 newtons generated with afterburner by the single Pratt & Whitney F135 engine powering the American F-35A.
While similar total thrust does not guarantee comparable flight performance, which also depends on aircraft weight and drag, it also remains unclear whether the WS-19 estimates and the F135’s afterburning thrust are measured on the same basis.
According to Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist in Chinese military aviation, future engine improvements could also reduce fuel consumption and improve reliability. Greater electrical output could support more demanding radar, electronic warfare and computing systems, although existing engine limitations remained unclear, he said.
China has previously introduced fighters with engines that were later replaced with more advanced models.
The J-10 and J-20 initially entered service with Russian-made engines before later versions adopted domestically developed power plants, including the WS-10, while the J-20A is now reported to be receiving the more powerful WS-15.
Beyond the engines, Shao suggested that carrying more weapons internally could expand the J-35A’s missions without compromising its low radar visibility, as externally mounted weapons can make stealth aircraft easier to detect.
[embedded media]
Rupprecht considered more capable weapons to be a priority. Future options could include more advanced air-to-air missiles, as well as cruise and anti-ship missiles designed to be difficult to detect, he said.
Peter Layton, a visiting fellow at Australia’s Griffith Asia Institute and a retired Royal Australian Air Force group captain, said he expected the J-35A to focus on air-defence missions, at least initially, intercepting enemy aircraft and protecting Chinese airspace.
The larger J-20 would be better suited to longer-range offensive operations, according to Layton.
Meanwhile, Rupprecht expects the smaller J-35A to become a widely used multi-role aircraft alongside the heavier J-20, gradually replacing much of China’s older fleet of J-11, early J-10 and JH-7A fighters.
If the J-35A assumes this broader role, it could eventually carry out a range of missions, from engaging enemy aircraft to striking targets on land and at sea, potentially offering a versatility similar to that of the American F-35.
Shao also suggested that J-35As could operate alongside J-20 fighters as well as uncrewed wingmen and airborne early-warning aircraft, sharing information to improve surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting.
Two other possibilities she raised were the development of a two-seater variant to command drones and a specialised electronic warfare version, although neither has been officially announced.
However, it remains unclear how quickly the J-35A could become a regular presence in PLA Air Force squadrons. While it entered service ahead of last year’s military parade in Beijing commemorating the end of World War II, that does not automatically mean full operational readiness.
A J-35A bearing the serial number 61821 was spotted taking part in the September 3 commemorations, with markings associated with the 1st Air Brigade, based in Anshan, northeastern China.
[embedded media]
According to Kadidal, the first production J-35As were assigned to the brigade by September 2025. However, it remains unclear whether the aircraft have entered routine squadron service or are still undergoing evaluation or training elsewhere.
China’s ability to deploy the J-35A in larger numbers will also depend on expanding production.
A satellite image taken in February and published in April showed the development of a new aircraft manufacturing complex north of Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning province in northeast China.
Michael Dahm, senior fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies and a former US Navy intelligence officer, assessed that the complex was probably intended to produce J-35 fighters for both the air and naval branches of the People’s Liberation Army.
A January assessment by Britain’s Royal United Services Institute said that while the J-35 family was almost certainly still in low-rate initial production in late 2025, output could increase rapidly over the coming years.
In Layton’s estimation, it could take roughly six more years before the J-35A enters regular squadron service. “I think the aircraft is not yet in operational standard service,” he said.
“The PLA Air Force previously has preferred a gradual and careful lead up to normal squadron service,” Layton added.
By Gabriel Dominguez

title_en: South Korea’s education chief has gone. Its AI exam headache has not
content_en:
A swift ministerial exit may shield Lee Jae Myung from voter anger, yet critics doubt ‘whack-a-mole’ bans can save an outdated exam.
South Korean students take a test in Seoul while wearing wearing aprons as part of measures to prevent the use of artificial intelligence to cheat. Photo: Yonhap/dpa
South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday days after the country’s national university entrance exam took place, in a move analysts see as an attempt to contain the fallout from a row over AI-assisted cheating before it damages the president’s already sagging approval ratings.
Choi Kyo-jin’s resignation, which was swiftly accepted by President Lee Jae Myung, has been widely interpreted as a de facto dismissal following the confusion surrounding anti-cheating measures for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), the single exam that largely decides university places in South Korea.
It was held last Thursday and passed without any major administrative disruptions, Choi said on Sunday while explaining his decision to resign. The ministry earlier announced that 111 test takers were caught violating smart-device rules, including five cases of active gadget use during the test.
Choi’s exit is expected to pave the way for a wider cabinet reshuffle, which could affect the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the National Intelligence Service, now that major recent diplomatic events such as last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen have concluded.
Exam-eve scramble
Two days before this year’s CSAT was set to be held, South Korea’s Education Ministry announced emergency measures.
These included:
Stickers to be placed over clothing buttons.
Inspections of glasses for hidden cameras.
A ban on mobile phones in exam rooms.
Thousands of additional invigilators, or exam supervisors.
Extra staff on hand to check for smart devices.
On the eve of the exam, the ministry also revised its guidelines regarding writing instruments to allow only black pencils. The last-minute change disrupted preparations at testing centres, with newly recruited invigilators having to receive emergency training by video call one day before the test was to be held.
Teachers’ unions have accused the government of failing to adequately prepare, and then shifting the blame onto educators who were recruited at short notice.
A proctor holds a metal detector at a secondary school in Seoul on Thursday, as students take the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. Photo: Korea Times
“Can someone who is hastily recruited as a proctor, trained the next day and deployed the day after that truly possess the expertise required to detect sophisticated, AI-driven cheating?” the Korean Federation of Teachers’ Associations asked in a statement.
Choi, who turns 73 on Tuesday, had already faced criticism over his answers about AI cheating to lawmakers. Last Monday, three days before the CSAT, Park Jung-hoon of the People Power Party asked whether the minister was confident that AI-assisted cheating could be detected with 100 per cent certainty.
“I don’t think I could,” Choi replied, adding: “Given my age.”
The reply drew immediate criticism, largely because the minister in charge of protecting the CSAT’s integrity had effectively just doubted his own ability to do so.
Announcing his departure on Sunday, Choi said: “As the minister in charge, I cannot escape the criticism that we failed to prepare adequately.” He credited the government’s preparations and the cooperation of exam takers, parents, invigilators and the public for what he described as the smooth running of this year’s CSAT.
Choi Kyo-jin, South Korea’s then education minister, faces questions about AI-related cheating at the National Assembly in Seoul on November 16. Photo: Yonhap/AP
Damage control
Choi Jin, head of the Institute of Presidential Leadership think tank, told This Week in Asia that university admissions were among South Korea’s most consequential hot-button issues.
“As in China, university admissions in South Korea are, in many ways, one of the country’s most significant national events,” he said, asking whether, given the minister’s “shortcomings, confusion and considerable incompetence”, dismissal was not “justified”.
He added that such a swift dismissal of a cabinet minister “embroiled in policy failures” could help “appease centrist voters” and shore up President Lee’s approval ratings that might otherwise have “remained stagnant”.
The fairness of national exams in South Korea had come under intense scrutiny after several AI-assisted cheating scandals – and subsequent crackdowns – involving the CSAT and professional licensing tests, said Cho Jin-man, a political-science professor at Duksung Women’s University.
President Lee took swift action to prevent the fallout from the controversy from damaging his political imageCho Jin-man, political-science professor
“Under these circumstances, President Lee took swift action to prevent the fallout from the controversy from damaging his political image,” Cho said. “The longer it takes to dismiss the minister, the greater the damage.”
Lee’s approval rating has fallen from a peak of about 65 per cent last year to around 40 per cent last week. Survey respondents mainly cite the economy and living costs as their biggest concerns. Specific complaints also include the handling of speculative stock market trading, inflation and persistently high youth unemployment.
Cho said the exam row could have added to mounting public discontent and heaped further pressure on Lee to act against the education minister.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung speaks at the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Thursday. The exam cheating controversy came at an unfortunate time for Lee, observers say. Photo: Xinhua
The controversy came at an unfortunate time for the president, whose ruling Democratic Party of Korea was already grappling with internal divisions. A faction aligned with Jung Chung-rae, a former party leader, has been at odds with the rival camp backing Lee. The Jung faction wants faster, more sweeping reforms, while the president favours a more moderate course.
Choi Jin said the question of who got to choose candidates for the next National Assembly election in 2028 was “at the root of their infighting”.
Lee Jae-mook, a political-science professor at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, forecast an impending cabinet reshuffle given that the current administration was less than halfway through its five-year term.
“A cabinet reshuffle could be a quick stopgap measure to prevent further political fallout from the examination controversy,” he said.
‘Whack-a-mole’ measures
The CSAT row also pointed to a larger problem, Lee Jae-mook said, as the test was essentially a multiple-choice exam that ranked students from first to more than 500,000th.
“AI is now fundamentally transforming the knowledge and education ecosystems themselves,” he said. “We need to engage in a fundamental rethink of what an appropriate assessment system should look like in the AI era.”
The centre-left Kyunghyang Shinmun newspaper made a similar argument in an editorial first published online on Sunday.
It said restoring public trust would be both a challenge and a test of whether South Korea’s government could move past its earlier failings. Tighter surveillance alone would not end cheating, it said, particularly as legal and institutional safeguards struggled to keep pace with rapid technological advancements.
A student waits for the start of the annual university entrance exams at an exam hall in Seoul, South Korea, on Thursday last week. Photo: Reuters
The newspaper urged a move towards teaching and educational assessments that rewarded problem solving rather than the quick selection of correct answers.
It further called for reform of a system in which rewards and opportunities disproportionately hinged on one or two exams.
“The greater the stakes … the stronger the temptation to resort to cheating,” it said in Korean, rejecting the view that grades were a direct indicator of ability.
“If the authorities continue to dodge these core issues and focus exclusively on blocking cheating – much like playing a game of ‘whack-a-mole’ – achieving fairness and public trust in our education and examination systems will remain a distant goal,” the editorial added.
By Park Chan-kyong

title_en: As Xi, Putin and Trump met in Shenzhen, EU’s absence was telling
content_en:
The conversation that mattered most took place in Shenzhen, while the call that shaped the discussions in Berlin came from Air Force One.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz dismissed the meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen as a photo opportunity. He has a point. The “peace declaration” issued by the three leaders contains few concrete commitments. The wars in Ukraine and Iran continue. Yet the first summit bringing together the presidents of China, Russia and the US produced more than a photograph.
For the first time, the heads of the world’s three largest nuclear powers sat at the same table and committed to reducing nuclear risks and preventing the further spread of nuclear weapons.
Xi went further, calling for their eventual abolition: “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.”
In Europe, where Moscow’s nuclear threats have loomed over the war since its earliest days, that message is welcome. But Beijing faces an obvious question. According to Pentagon estimates, China is on course to have 1,000 operational warheads by 2030. A country calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons is building more of them.
As the three leaders met in Shenzhen, European governments gathered in Berlin. Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted dozens of heads of state and government to discuss further support for Ukraine.
Merz warned that “a ‘Yalta’ format will not bring peace”, invoking the 1945 conference at which the victors of the second world war divided Europe into spheres of influence. Britain still had a place at the table in Berlin, while in Shenzhen, no European leader was present. The shift in the balance of power could hardly have been clearer.
US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on November 19. Photo: AP
Then Trump called. On his flight home aboard Air Force One, he joined the meeting reportedly via his son-in-law Jared Kushner’s phone. Kushner was sitting in the German Federal Chancellery alongside Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff.
According to participants, Trump told the Europeans that Putin “wants to end the war”. Several accounts also say he questioned the billions being spent in aid for Kyiv and pointed out how much money could be saved if the fighting stopped. Around the same time, Putin declared in Shenzhen that there would be no ceasefire, directly contradicting the US president.
More than three decades after the end of the Cold War, Europe can pledge billions to Ukraine and bring dozens of world leaders to Berlin. Yet the conversation that mattered most took place in Shenzhen, while the call that shaped the discussions in Berlin came from Air Force One.
On the war that most directly affects its own security, Europe still depends on an American president who calls Putin a “friend” and rates the meeting with him and Xi “a 12” on a scale of zero to 10. On the other hand, Trump berates European leaders regularly.
There were, however, some encouraging signs in Berlin. Kushner told the Europeans that Trump “wants to make a deal with Europe by his side” and does not seek to “impose anything unilaterally”. He and Witkoff then spent several more hours with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the national security advisers of Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Poland. Europe still doesn’t have one single voice on these matters.
Burnham described the discussions as the first real alignment between the United States and Europe on Ukraine in months. Putin, for his part, said publicly in Shenzhen that he was open to the Europeans joining the peace talks. But any role for Europe at the negotiating table would depend on Moscow’s consent and Washington’s backing. It has yet to establish one for itself.
(From left) German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, French President Emmanuel Macron and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave after a joint press conference at the “Coalition of the Willing” summit at the Chancellery in Berlin on November 19. Photo: Reuters
The next test may come sooner than expected. Trump has invited Putin to the G20 summit at his golf resort in Miami in December and is expected to meet Xi there as well. Such encounters are beyond Europe’s control. What European governments can still determine is whether they have enough political and economic weight to influence what comes out of them.
That requires a more direct approach to Beijing. Xi’s opposition to the use of nuclear weapons offers one of the few areas of common ground between China and Europe over the war in Ukraine. European governments should make more of it and engage with Beijing directly, rather than rely on Washington to convey their concerns. China remains Russia’s most important economic partner.
A serious appeal from Beijing for a ceasefire would carry considerably more weight in the Kremlin than another declaration at an international summit. Europe would have to be prepared to offer something in return, perhaps on trade where relations have been strained for years.
Berlin has already set out some of the other priorities. A proposed €45 billion (US$49 billion) in aid for Ukraine needs to be delivered. The plans for a multinational force to support post-war Ukraine’s economic security require further work. Europe’s defence industry also needs to expand.
Without these capabilities, European governments will struggle to influence negotiations over their own security. A stronger Europe would also be a more credible partner for Beijing. China has little interest in being friends with the US alone, and a Europe capable of acting independently could become a much more useful counterpart.
Xi, Putin and Trump may meet again in Miami in December. Europe is likely to have a seat at the table at this year’s G20 summit. The question is whether it will have enough influence to shape what is decided there, or whether the crucial terms will have been settled before the Europeans arrive.
By Alexander Görlach

title_en: China’s shipbuilders turn to bankrupt, idle yards for rapid expansion amid booming market
content_en:
China Merchants Shipbuilding expanded its capacity through an equity deal with the bankrupt Quanzhou Shipyard in Fujian province.
The Qingshan Shipyard on the Yangtze River in Wuhan, in the central province of Hubei. Photo: Handout
Amid a shipbuilding boom and intense competition, Chinese shipyards are adopting a faster route to gain market share: doing deals with bankrupt or long-idled facilities.
“Compared with building from scratch, reviving idle or bankrupt assets is far faster,” said Zhong Zhechao, a Shanghai-based independent shipping analyst. “Chinese shipyards are placing greater emphasis on efficiency as they seek to capture market share amid the extended shipbuilding upcycle.”
Supply continues to lag demand across China’s shipbuilding sector. Hong Kong-based Goldman Sachs analysts led by Herbert Lu wrote in a Friday research note that site visits to major mainland shipyards showed capacity remained tight, with order books fully booked through 2029, and in some cases to 2030.
Management teams expected the robust demand to persist until 2032 or 2035, the note said.
Against this backdrop, several acquisitions of idle shipyards assets have been closed so far this year.
China Merchants Shipbuilding, the world’s fourth-largest shipbuilder by compensated gross tonnage orders, struck an equity deal for Quanzhou Shipyard in Fujian province, opening the door for the yard to add new shipbuilding capability to its existing ship-repair operations.
The shipyard was founded in 2004 and filed for bankruptcy in 2019, according to local media reports. The tie-up comes with an initial offer for six world-first 343,000 deadweight tonnage (dwt) very large ore carriers, according to a China Merchants statement.
In February, China Merchants Group took over the Wuhan Qingshan Shipyard located on the Yangtze River in Hubei province. The yard had suspended newbuilding work eight years earlier.
Actual capacity figures were not disclosed for either project.
Buoyant profits and unresolved geopolitical tensions will keep capacity expansion going in the near termZhong Zhechao, independent shipping analyst
“Efficiency is just one factor. Another driver behind this restructuring wave is that older yards boast hard-to-replicate advantages in location, shipping channels and existing infrastructure,” Zhong added.
Quanzhou Shipyard has been touted as one of Asia’s largest integrated ship repair and newbuilding complexes by local media. A Wednesday report from Quanzhou Evening Post noted the yard sits at one of China’s few ice-free, silt-free deepwater berths capable of handling 300,000 dwt vessels.
As fresh orders continue to come in, Chinese firms are also deploying capital to build new capacity.

title_en: China stock support steadies market after AI-fuelled selling
content_en:
Mainland regulators moved to prop up shares after a global rout in artificial intelligence stocks last week.
Photo: EPA
Chinese stocks stabilised on Monday as government support buttressed the market after a global artificial intelligence (AI) rout.
The CSI300 Index closed little changed, after earlier falling as much as 1.3 per cent. Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index and the Hang Seng Tech Index both fell about 0.1 per cent.
Mainland China, South Korea and Taiwan all took steps to prop up shares over the weekend after growing concerns about AI demand and profits hammered markets around the world last week. The Nasdaq 100 suffered its biggest weekly drop since March 2020, and Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled the most in about 35 years, as a sentiment boost from Anthropic’s mega IPO quickly wore off amid tighter US chip export controls, growing opposition to data centres and the defenestration of Jensen Huang at Nvidia.
China’s market support efforts included freeing up 400 billion yuan (US$60 billion) in liquidity by announcing a reduction in minimum margin requirements for stock financing to 80 per cent from 100 per cent starting November 30.
The change would “improve market liquidity and support the market’s long-term stability and healthy development”, according to statements on Sunday from the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges. The minimum was raised to 100 per cent in January to curb speculation.
China’s national team of state investment funds also poured a record 90 billion yuan into nine exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on Friday, according to Bloomberg News, to help the market. The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges announced about 2.75 billion yuan of stock-trading fee discounts on Sunday, along with initiatives to boost market-making activity on the tech-focused Star and ChiNext Markets.
[embedded media]
Related news:
Taiwan’s Taiex index rose by 2.2 per cent on Monday after the island unveiled five measures on Saturday to “maintain the order and stability of the securities market”. These included a complete ban on short selling below the previous trading day’s closing price and an adjustment of the minimum margin to 150 per cent from 130 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi dropped by 3.3 per cent even as authorities eased daily limits on company share buy-backs for three months and began preparations to potentially activate a stock-market stabilisation fund.
Mainland Chinese regulators last week ramped up a campaign against false online rumours that could rattle markets by releasing a dossier outlining cases where content creators were penalised. Examples included fake news on tax policies and stock market listings. Earlier in the week, the China Securities Regulatory Commission also debunked a rumour that it had ordered mutual funds to report their exposures to the AI sector. Elsewhere, consumer stocks have bucked the China sell-off, with investors lured by discounts of about 30 per cent versus global peers. Consumer staples have risen by 12 per cent since the end of September.
Mainland China’s top state planner urged local authorities to accelerate construction of government investment projects and hasten fund disbursements to spur economic growth. There should also be more monitoring and coordination among local authorities to increase on-the-ground activity, the National Development and Reform Commission said on Saturday. Local officials were instructed to boost preparatory works and enhance strategic planning to improve the quality of projects in the pipeline.
How others reported it
Worrying sign: A big difference, so far, is that the dot-com bust led to a recession, which contributed to weakness in sectors otherwise unaffected and spurred another deep sell-off in 2001. The unknown now is whether the sell-off continues, as it did then. The market’s failure to rally after the successful IPO of Anthropic on Thursday isn’t a good sign, but at least for now the economy appears robust. (The Wall Street Journal)
Margin support: “The support measures appear more sentiment- and liquidity-oriented than fundamentally market-changing,” said Fu Zhifeng, chief investment officer at Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management. “The market-making measure may provide only marginal liquidity support, while lowering the minimum margin requirement for securities financing from 100 per cent to 80 per cent mainly eases near-term forced-selling pressure and provides investors more time to meet margin calls, rather than bringing meaningful new capital into the market.” (Bloomberg)
Interconnected: There’s another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia … This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis. (NPR)
Market impact: “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” (Associated Press)
Tighter controls: “Closing the [China-US AI] gap at ⁠the leading edge before 2028, or even by 2030, looks difficult,” Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research, said of the impact of US measures on China’s AI industry. The impact would be “far more prominent” in frontier model training than in inference, Shah said, adding that AI start-ups such as Moonshot AI, Z.AI, MiniMax and DeepSeek were more likely to be hit harder than hyperscalers such as Alibaba and Tencent. (Reuters)
The SCMP Plus takeaway
Investors gorged on AI shares in the first half of the year. These days, they have lost their appetite.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Tech Index has slumped by 41 per cent from its January high, wiping out all the gains from a China stocks bull market launched by the central bank two years ago.
Shenzhen’s ChiNext is down by 29 per cent for the year, even with Monday’s rebound. A 36 per cent surge in the first half of the year has long since been erased. It’s the same story for Shanghai’s Star 50 Index. A first-half gain of 64 per cent has now turned into an 8.7 per cent loss for the year to date.
Combined, the three indices had shed US$1.7 trillion in market value since the end of June as of Friday, according to Bloomberg News.
Still, Chinese tech stocks are not alone. The Nasdaq lost about 10 per cent last week and the S&P 500 posted its poorest showing since Donald Trump launched his global trade war in April 2025. Anthropic’s mammoth initial public offering only provided a brief respite as the stock lost 8.5 per cent on Friday eroding most of the gains from a debut rally a day earlier.
In Asia, this year’s gains for South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index have slumped to 12 per cent from as much as 116 per cent amid routs for chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Taiwan’s Taiex had its biggest weekly decline since 1991 last week, dragged down by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The chipmaking giant makes up about half of the index by market capitalisation.
Still, the Kospi and Taiex both remain up for the year, which is more than can be said for markets in mainland China and Hong Kong.
The global sell-off has been driven in part by increasing investor queasiness over the steep costs of the AI buildout. There are also concerns about US companies being left paying for equipment they can’t use after popular opposition to power-hungry and noisy data centres helped the Democrats gain control of both the House and Senate in midterm elections.
The US Federal Reserve further rattled markets when minutes from its October policy meeting were released on Wednesday. These indicated that nearly all members foresee interest rate increases to rein in inflation driven by tariffs, higher energy costs and upwards pressure on consumer goods prices due to the AI buildout.
Jensen Huang’s departure earlier this month from Nvidia amid a spy scandal has hit the chip giant and the wider AI sector. The company’s shares slumped by 14 per cent on Friday, capping a sixth straight weekly decline even after better-than-expected results.
Huang’s downfall has sparked concerns about broader AI investment as he had turned Nvidia into the sector’s “central bank”. The chipmaker has invested billions across the industry, effectively supporting customers’ purchases of its chips and driving up wider AI spending.
That funding may now be in doubt, as interim chief executive Colette Kress has said that Nvidia will take a “very strong look” at who it helps out. A pullback by the chip giant would quickly work its way down the AI supply chain.
The Nvidia upheavals have had a particularly strong impact on Chinese AI companies as Huang was a major advocate of letting them buy and access high-end US chips. His departure has removed a key counterweight to China hawks. The spy accusations, which China has denied, also contributed to a clampdown on Chinese companies using overseas data centres to get round US export controls.
Tech giants Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent have all fallen by at least 10 per cent in Hong Kong trading since Huang resigned. The three companies make up 20.8 per cent of the Hang Seng Tech Index’s effective weighting. The gauge has an 8 per cent single-stock weighting cap. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
China’s bruised investors are seeking shelter from the hi-tech storm by buying into previously maligned, low-tech consumer stocks. Shanghai-listed liquor maker Kweichow Moutai was the most popular stock addition to 18 new actively managed ETFs approved by the securities watchdog last month, followed by home-appliance maker Midea Group.
